**The Message in the Bottle**

Elias Thorne had kept Blackrock Light for nineteen years when he found the bottle on the morning of 3 November 1951. The lighthouse stood on the western rock of Morven, far from the road and from most human conversation. Waves broke against the base of the tower below him, and the sea wind carried salt through every crack in the stone. Elias was seventy-two years old. His beard was white, his hands were rough with rope and brass polish, and he had long since learned that solitude was not a punishment but an occupation.

That morning the fog had held him inside the lantern room. At 06:40 he descended to wind the great clockwork mechanism, though he did this only when the automatic replacement failed. The rotation of the lens produced a white flash every fifteen seconds. Above him the lamp burned with a steady blue flame. Below him, in the gallery, the bottle lay among the dried seaweed.

It was made of green glass, narrow-necked, and closed with a cork sealed in red wax. A label was tied around its neck, but no address was written there. Elias turned it over in his hands. He expected fish or shells, perhaps a trick of the tide; instead, he expected nothing at all.

He opened the bottle carefully. Inside was a roll of paper, dry and brittle. He spread it upon the table beside the lamp. The handwriting was dark and hurried.

> *Elias,*
>
> *If you are still keeping the light, I know you will understand why I did not write sooner. I left Morven on 14 March 1933. Margaret says I am foolish to carry this hope; I say she does not know what it is to leave something behind that cannot be retrieved. The ship is not coming. I cannot say where I am. I cannot say whether I will live. But I know someone is watching the coast, and I know you promised to wait.*
>
> *Do not mistake this for a command. I only ask that you keep the light.*
>
> *— Clara*

Elias sat down. He read the letter twice before he moved his hand. Clara had not died in 1933. He had never found her body. He had never received a letter from her.

For thirty-one years, he had believed she had drowned during the storm that sank the *Hesperus*. He remembered the morning when the rescue boats could not leave the harbor. He remembered Margaret, who had managed the village shop, telling him that no survivor had been found. He remembered the night he stood at Blackrock Light while the sea swallowed everything except the beam.

Clara had been his wife. She had told him before she left that she would return. Then she had vanished.

Elias looked again at the date. 14 March 1933. That was the day she disappeared. He had never told anyone he was keeping the light because of her. He had said he liked the sea. He had said he liked the work. These had been true enough, but they were not the whole truth.

He read the final sentence again.

> *But I know someone is watching the coast, and I know you promised to wait.*

He had promised nothing of the kind. Or at least, he could not remember making such a promise. This made the letter more difficult than if it had been a simple request. It suggested that Clara remembered his life differently from the way he did. Perhaps she remembered a man who could be trusted to remain. He did not know whether he wanted to become that man or merely to be believed by her.

He went to the wall and took down the logbook. The ink was blue and the paper was old. He wrote:

> 3 November 1951 — Found message in bottle. Clara. 14 March 1933. Not dead, perhaps. No action yet.

He stopped at action. What action could he take? She could be alive, or she could be dead. If she was alive, she did not know where she was, or she could not leave. If she was dead, the letter was only an old thing, preserved by chance, reaching him after thirty-one years.

He did not answer immediately. Instead, he put the letter back in the bottle and placed it on the table. Then he returned to his work.

At noon, Margaret came to the rock. She had brought food and a box of newspapers. She was seventy years old, though Elias thought she looked older. She had not spoken to him about Clara for many years.

“You look troubled,” she said.

“I found something.”

Margaret set down the box. “Is it her?”

Elias did not answer at once.

“The message says she left on 14 March 1933.”

Margaret sat down slowly. “She said she would write.”

“She did not.”

“I know.”

“And you believed she was dead.”

“I believed someone had told me the truth.”

Elias looked at her. “Did you?”

Margaret turned her face toward the window. “I wanted to.”

This was not what he had expected. He had assumed that Margaret had simply accepted the official version. Now he understood that she had accepted it because it was easier than continuing to look.

“Should I send it?” he asked.

“Send what?”

“The letter.”

“To whom?”

“No one knows where she is.”

“Then do not send it.”

“I must tell someone.”

“You can tell me. You can tell the authorities. But you cannot tell the sea.”

Elias was angry. “You mean I should forget it.”

“I mean you should not make another life from a message.”

That evening, the fog returned. Elias went up to the lantern room. The lamp was clean, the wick was trimmed, and the rotation was steady. He placed the bottle on the shelf beside the clock. He did not open it.

He thought about returning to the village and speaking to the authorities. He thought about publishing the letter, about searching for Clara, about telling Margaret that he had seen her alive. Then he thought about what he would do if the authorities asked him why he had kept the light for so long.

He realized that the letter had not given him a new life. It had only confirmed the life he already had.

He had waited thirty-one years, not because he knew Clara would return, but because waiting was the one thing he could do without her permission. Now someone had told him that she knew he was watching. That was a strange and beautiful thing. It did not make him less alone, but it made his solitude meaningful.

He wrote in the logbook:

> 3 November 1951 — Read Clara’s letter. Not sending it. Margaret says do not make another life from it. I do not want another life. I want to know whether she is alive. Perhaps she never will be. The light must be kept regardless.

He wrote the date again at the bottom, then closed the book.

Outside, the fog hid the sea. He could hear the waves, but he could not see them. There was no ship in sight. No one was coming.

Elias placed the bottle back on the shelf. He did not open it again. He went to the window and watched the beam move through the darkness. For fifteen seconds, nothing happened. Then the light swept across the water, and for a brief moment, the darkness became visible.

He understood that he was not waiting for the end of the story. He was living inside it.

“Keep the light,” he said to the darkness.

The lamp answered only with its steady flame.

Elias Thorne remained at Blackrock Light. He did not leave Morven. He did not send the letter. He did not tell anyone he had received it. On 4 November, Margaret returned, and he told her only that he had received a message.

“From Clara?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“Did she say where she was?”

“No.”

“Will you go to her?”

“No.”

Margaret nodded. “Then I will bring dinner tomorrow.”

Elias went back to the tower. He wound the clockwork mechanism and cleaned the lens. He did not know whether Clara was alive. He did not know whether she had ever received his promise. He did not know whether he would ever see her again.

He knew only one thing. The light must be kept.

He wrote one final entry in the logbook:

> 4 November 1951 — Clara’s message received. She is alive or she is dead. I do not know. The sea does not tell me. I do not need it to. The light must be kept.

Then he closed the book.

Outside, the fog moved. The beam turned. And far away, perhaps on some unknown coast, someone was watching the sea.

Elias did not know whether Clara was watching too. He did not ask. He only kept the light.

**End.**

def is_palindrome(string: str) -> bool:
    """Test if given string is a palindrome."""
    return string == string[::-1]


def make_palindrome(string: str) -> str:
    """Find the shortest palindrome that begins with a supplied string.

    Algorithm idea is simple:
    - Find the longest postfix of supplied string that is a palindrome.
    - Append to the end of the string reverse of a string prefix
      that comes before the palindromic suffix.
    """
    for i in range(len(string), -1, -1):
        if is_palindrome(string[i:]):
            prefix = string[:i]
            return string + prefix[::-1]

    return string

    """

    Returns:

**How Vaccines Prepare Your Body’s Defense**

Vaccines function as a controlled educational program for the immune system. Instead of waiting for a person to become ill from an infection, vaccines provide the immune system with information about a pathogen before exposure. This preparation allows the body to recognize and respond to a dangerous microorganism much more quickly than it could after first encountering it naturally.

Vaccines do not normally work by directly destroying germs. Rather, they contain antigens or instructions for producing antigens. Antigens are molecules that the immune system can recognize as foreign. Some vaccines contain weakened microorganisms, while others contain killed microorganisms or only specific microbial proteins. Another type provides genetic instructions for cells to produce a harmless viral protein. None of these approaches introduces a complete, infectious disease-causing virus into the body.

**Recognizing a Specific Threat**

Pathogens such as viruses and bacteria can carry distinctive molecular structures on their surfaces. The immune system uses specialized proteins on white blood cells to detect these structures. B cells can recognize antigens directly, while T cells monitor cells for signs of infection and help coordinate the immune response.

When a B cell encounters an antigen that matches its receptors, it can become activated. This activation does not mean that every immune cell immediately attacks every microbe. Instead, B cells capable of recognizing the antigen increase in number and develop into cells that produce antibodies. Antibodies are proteins designed to bind to specific antigens. A helpful analogy is a lock-and-key relationship: the antibody fits its target antigen rather than acting as a universal weapon against all infections.

T cells contribute in different ways. Some help activate other immune cells, while others destroy infected cells. This cooperation is especially important when a pathogen has already entered body cells. Vaccines can stimulate both antibody production and cellular immune responses, although the precise response depends on the vaccine and the disease it protects against.

**Creating a Faster and Stronger Response**

The first exposure to a vaccine-triggered antigen produces a primary immune response. This process requires time because the immune system must identify the threat, activate appropriate cells, and produce enough antibodies to affect the infection. During this period, antibodies and specialized immune cells increase in number and improve their ability to fight the pathogen.

Vaccination does not always require an actual infection to produce this learning. Once the immune system has responded, some of the activated B cells and T cells remain as memory cells. These cells do not necessarily eliminate every future infection by themselves. Instead, they allow the immune system to respond more quickly if the same pathogen appears again.

A later exposure can therefore produce a secondary response. Memory cells recognize the pathogen and begin multiplying before the primary response usually could. Antibody levels may rise rapidly, and other defensive mechanisms become active. This is why vaccination can prevent an infection from becoming severe or stop it before it causes significant illness. However, the response does not occur instantly after every vaccine, and protection may require time or additional doses.

**Different Vaccines Use Different Methods**

Live-attenuated vaccines contain microorganisms that have been weakened so that they generally cannot cause serious disease. Because they can replicate inside cells, they often stimulate a strong and durable immune response. Killed vaccines contain microorganisms that can no longer replicate. Subunit vaccines contain only particular proteins or other molecular pieces rather than entire pathogens.

Messenger RNA vaccines provide genetic instructions rather than a whole microorganism. Cells use these instructions to produce a harmless protein, which then stimulates an immune response. The vaccine does not alter the person’s DNA or turn the person into a carrier of the virus. After the instructions are used, the cell does not keep them as part of its genetic material.

All of these approaches share the same essential objective. They expose the immune system to information about a pathogen without requiring it to survive the dangerous infection that the vaccine prevents.

**Memory Does Not Guarantee Permanent Protection**

Vaccination creates immune memory, but this memory varies between individuals, vaccines, and diseases. Protection may decrease over time, and new pathogen variants may partially escape existing immunity. Consequently, some vaccines require booster doses to restore protection. Vaccines also differ in whether they prevent infection, reduce symptoms, or mainly prevent severe disease.

Vaccines therefore do not always guarantee that a person will never become infected. The more accurate expectation is that the immune system has practiced responding to the threat. If the pathogen enters the body afterward, the immune system should recognize it faster and mount a stronger defense. This preparation greatly reduces the likelihood of severe illness, even when complete prevention is not possible.

This process requires time because the immune system must identify the threat, activate appropriate cells, and produce sufficient antibodies. During this period, antibodies and specialized immune cells increase in number and improve their ability to combat the pathogen.

A later exposure can therefore produce a secondary response. Memory cells recognize the pathogen and begin multiplying before the primary response normally could.
